Nagykallo New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Nagykálló, Hungary

Not demolished. Nagykálló, former county seat of Szabolcs, was home to a Jewish community from its early days; the town's most significant religious figure, Isaac Taub (Yitzchak Taub), elected chief rabbi in 1781, founded Hungary's first Hasidic community and drew followers from across the region until his death in 1821. Painter Ámos Imre - often called 'the Hungarian Chagall,' known for works drawing on Hasidic and everyday Jewish life - was also born there, dying in forced labor in 1944. Population reached 982 members by 1929 (165 taxpayers), engaged across trades, law, medicine, and farming; by 1941, 869 of the town's 9,863 residents were Jewish. The main synagogue, built around 1800 and expanded in 1924, operated until 1956, with a handful of postwar survivors still praying there until its 1960 demolition - locals repurposed its bricks for houses and barns, though the Torah ark and a row of benches were saved, and one wall still stands on Várkert Street. This newer cemetery, established by 1828, remained active through at least 1944, with an unexplained final burial as late as 1999; it was fenced in 1986, and several bullet-damaged tombstones bear likely WWII-era scars.
